entities.name: Emperor Xizong of Tang
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Emperor Xizong of Tang (né Li Yan, later Li Xuan), who reigned from 873 to 888, presided over a period of catastrophic decline that irrevocably shattered the centralized authority of China's Tang dynasty. Ascending to the throne as the fifth son of Emperor Yizong, Xizong inherited a realm already reeling from economic distress, entrenched eunuch power, and widespread official corruption. His reign is primarily defined by the devastating agrarian rebellions led by Wang Xianzhi and, more famously, Huang Chao, which fundamentally undermined the Tang state and foreshadowed its eventual collapse. These widespread insurrections, fueled by famine and heavy taxation, exposed the profound fragility of the imperial administration and its inability to maintain control over its vast territories.

The core events of Xizong's emperorship were dominated by the relentless advance of the Huang Chao Rebellion. Beginning in 874, this peasant uprising spiraled out of control, sweeping across central and southern China. In 880, Huang Chao's forces captured the imperial capital, Chang'an, forcing Emperor Xizong to flee in ignominy to Chengdu in Sichuan. The rebels occupied Chang'an for three years, during which time they ransacked the city, destroyed much of its infrastructure, and established a short-lived rival dynasty. Although imperial and regional forces eventually dislodged Huang Chao in 883, leading to his ultimate defeat and death in 884, the central government's prestige and power were irreparably damaged, and its treasury depleted.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Emperor Xizong's reign marks a critical turning point in Chinese history, as the catastrophic Huang Chao Rebellion permanently shattered the Tang dynasty's central authority, directly leading to the fragmentation of the empire and setting the stage for the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.
